questions.q: Which vernacular term corresponds to Flush?
questions.ref: Common Philippine construction vernacular; no single authoritative standard, and usage may vary by region and practitioner.
questions.n: “Alahado” = flush. Likely from Spanish alisado “smoothed” (alisar = to smooth, level). The exact form is unconfirmed.

questions.q: In Philippine construction vernacular, Door fillet is called:
questions.ref: Common Philippine construction vernacular; no single authoritative standard, and usage may vary by region and practitioner. Figure: Know-How Architecture InstaFlashCards.
questions.n: “Batidora” = door fillet. Likely from Spanish batir “to beat, strike”, the strip a door strikes against. Don't confuse Batidora (door fillet) with Batidura (astragal, fillet).

questions.q: What is the vernacular term for Window sill?
questions.ref: Common Philippine construction vernacular; no single authoritative standard, and usage may vary by region and practitioner. Figure: Know-How Architecture InstaFlashCards.
questions.n: “Pasamano” = window sill. Origin: Spanish pasamano, from pasar “to pass” + mano “hand”. It is a rail or ledge you run or rest your hand along.

questions.q: What is the vernacular term for Door head?
questions.ref: Common Philippine construction vernacular; no single authoritative standard, and usage may vary by region and practitioner.
questions.n: “Sombrero Pintuan” = door head. Origin: Spanish sombrero “hat”. The head is the hat on top of the door.

questions.q: What is the vernacular term for Jamb (window or door jamb)?
questions.ref: Common Philippine construction vernacular; no single authoritative standard, and usage may vary by region and practitioner. Figure: Know-How Architecture InstaFlashCards.
questions.n: “Hamba” = jamb (window or door jamb). Origin: Spanish jamba “jamb”. Filipino spelling turns j into h, as in jamba, hamba.

questions.q: In Philippine construction vernacular, Transom is called:
questions.ref: Common Philippine construction vernacular; no single authoritative standard, and usage may vary by region and practitioner.
questions.n: “Espeho” = transom. Likely origin: Spanish espejo “mirror”, since transoms are often a glass panel over the door.

questions.q: Which vernacular term corresponds to Groove?
questions.ref: Common Philippine construction vernacular; no single authoritative standard, and usage may vary by region and practitioner. Figure: Know-How Architecture InstaFlashCards.
questions.n: “Kanal / Canal” = groove. Origin: Spanish canal “channel”. A groove is a small channel cut in the wood. The same term is also used for: gutter.

questions.q: What is the vernacular term for Miter?
questions.ref: Common Philippine construction vernacular; no single authoritative standard, and usage may vary by region and practitioner. Figure: Know-How Architecture InstaFlashCards.
questions.n: “Canto Mesa / Kanto Mesa” = miter. Likely from Spanish canto “edge, corner” + mesa “table”: the neat corner joint of a table or frame.

questions.q: What is the vernacular term for Rabbet joint?
questions.ref: Common Philippine construction vernacular; no single authoritative standard, and usage may vary by region and practitioner.
questions.n: “Vaciada” = rabbet joint. Origin: Spanish vaciado “hollowed out”, from vaciar “to empty”. A rabbet is a hollowed-out step cut into the wood.

questions.q: Which vernacular term corresponds to Panel door?
questions.ref: Common Philippine construction vernacular; no single authoritative standard, and usage may vary by region and practitioner. Figure: Know-How Architecture InstaFlashCards.
questions.n: “de Bandeha” = panel door. Origin: likely Spanish de bandeja “tray-like”. The recessed panels look like trays.

questions.q: In Philippine construction vernacular, Window head is called:
questions.ref: Common Philippine construction vernacular; no single authoritative standard, and usage may vary by region and practitioner.
questions.n: “Sumbrero” = window head. Origin: Spanish sombrero “hat”. The head is the hat on top of the window.

questions.q: In Philippine construction vernacular, Weatherstrip is called:
questions.ref: Common Philippine construction vernacular; no single authoritative standard, and usage may vary by region and practitioner.
questions.n: “Baryete” = weatherstrip. Likely origin: Spanish burlete “weatherstrip, draught excluder”. Baryete is burlete reshaped.

questions.q: Which vernacular term corresponds to Door jamb?
questions.ref: Common Philippine construction vernacular; no single authoritative standard, and usage may vary by region and practitioner. Figure: Know-How Architecture InstaFlashCards.
questions.n: “Hamba Pintuan” = door jamb. Origin: Spanish jamba “jamb”. Filipino spelling turns j into h, as in jamba, hamba.
